\documentclass{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Low-Cost Time-Lapse Cameras for Snowpack Monitoring:\newline Eleven Melt Seasons in the Kyrgyz Tien Shan}
\author{D.~A.~Rysbekova, P.~J.~Whitfield, and L.~Moreau}
\date{March 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Snowpack observations in high Central Asia are sparse, and it's hard to plan reservoir releases without them.
We deployed a network of 38 cameras across one headwater catchment and followed the snowpack for 11 melt seasons.
The cameras recorded snow depth daily at a fraction of the cost of telemetry stations.
Snow-depth retrievals matched manual surveys within a few centimetres for most of the season.
Melt-out dates at the upper site came pretty much two weeks earlier over the record.
The network shows that time-lapse photography can carry routine monitoring in remote terrain.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Seasonal snow is the main water store for the rivers of Central Asia.
Irrigation calendars and reservoir rule curves both depend on the timing of the melt.
Yet the observation network above 2,500 m is thin and getting thinner.
Automatic stations with weighing lysimeters and ultrasonic rangers are costly to install and to keep running.
Telemetry fails when solar panels ice over or when masts are buried.
Park rangers don't visit the high basins between November and April.
Manual snow courses still exist, but they are spaced a month apart and miss storm cycles.
The data gap is a big deal for the agencies that schedule spring releases.
Satellite products help, though clouds and steep terrain limit their use in narrow valleys.
A cheap complement comes from consumer cameras, since time lapse imagery needs no telemetry.
A camera with a battery and a memory card can run for a full winter without service.
Stakes placed in the field of view give a scale for snow depth.
Repeat photographs also document snow-cover extent on the surrounding slopes.
Several research groups have shown the approach in the Alps and the Rockies.
Those installations were mostly single cameras near roads or huts.
Whether a large network can survive a Central Asian winter was less clear.
This paper reports on more than a decade of camera observations in one Kyrgyz headwater catchment.
We describe the network design, the field protocol, and the retrieval method.
We compare the retrievals with manual surveys and with a conventional station.
We close with costs, failure modes, and recommendations for operators.

\section{Snow and Climate Context}
Winter precipitation at the outlet gauge averages 410 millimetres.
The wettest winters in the record brought late spring storms.
The driest winters still left a continuous pack at the upper sites.
Snow cover at the camera sites lasts from late October to June.
The pack at the lower sites ripens within days of the last storm.
The upper pack can stay cold through April.
Rain-on-snow events occur most often in March.
The 2018 event flooded the lower meadows for a week.
Summer snowfall is common above 3,000 m.
These events reset the surface but melt within days.
The basin loses its seasonal cover completely by early July.
Glacier melt sustains flow through the late summer.
The agency separates snowmelt and glacier melt in its forecasts.
The camera record covers only the seasonal pack.
Winters with thin early snow show the deepest ground frost.
Herders report harder spring forage after such winters.
The climate context here is continental and dry.
Interannual variability is large, which motivates long records.

\section{Study Area}
The study catchment drains the northern slope of the Terskey Ala-Too range.
The instrumented area lies between 2,480 m and 3,120 m above sea level.
The main camera basin is a very open glacial trough with gentle side slopes.
The gauge hut stands at 2,860 m beside a moraine lake.
The catchment channel runs 4.1 km from the glacier snout to the lake outlet.
Winter precipitation falls mostly as snow between October and May.
Summer storms bring rain at lower elevations and wet snow near the divide.
Vegetation is alpine meadow with juniper shrubs on the stony slopes.
A herding track crosses the basin and is used from June to September.
The nearest roadhead is a half day away by four-wheel drive.
Power and network coverage end at the valley mouth.
The regional water agency maintains a staffed gauge at the lake outlet.
The gauge record begins in 1964 and continues today.
Snow courses on the side slopes were measured monthly until 1991 and resumed in 2015.
The basin was chosen because the camera views stay free of avalanche paths.
Two small hanging glaciers feed the upper tributaries.
Rock glaciers line the shaded side of the trough.
The frozen ground under the meadows thaws through June.
The lake outlet marks the lowest point of the instrumented area.
Slopes above the meadow bench are mostly free of trees.
Avalanche paths were mapped from archival photographs before siting.
No camera looks across a mapped path.

\section{Camera Network}
The network grew from a pilot pair of cameras to 38 stations over four years.
Sites were chosen for open views of the meadow and the drift zones.
Each station pairs a camera with a two-metre painted stake.
The stakes carry decimetre bands that the retrieval code reads directly.
Cameras store one image per hour on industrial memory cards.
A ten-watt solar panel charges a small lithium battery through winter.
The housings are steel boxes with a glass port and a silica gel cartridge.
A desiccant cartridge won't stop fogging if the seal is damaged.
Mounting posts are angled steel driven a metre into the ground.
Guy wires keep the posts steady in valley winds.
The cameras use a fixed focus and a fixed exposure programme.
A time-lapse interval of one hour was chosen as a compromise between storage and resolution.
The timelapse mode also records a calibration frame at noon each day.
The time-lapse schedule was shortened to thirty minutes during the melt weeks.
Each site visit follows a fixed loop of the basin.
The loop takes two long days on foot in spring conditions.
The cameras run a sort of sleep mode between frames.
Sites near the herding track are checked more often.
A snow pillow at the central site provides an independent reference.
The pillow signal is logged every fifteen minutes and transmitted in summer.
Camera clocks drift, so the timestamps are corrected against the logger at each visit.
Station names follow the tributary and the altitude.
The full station list sits in the project archive.

\section{Field Protocol}
Visits begin with a condition check of the housing and the post.
The team cleans the glass port and replaces the desiccant.
Memory cards are swapped and sealed in labelled envelopes.
Battery voltage and panel current are read with a handheld meter.
The stake is brushed down and photographed from the camera position.
Snow depth at the stake is read by eye and written in the field book.
A second reading is taken at a marked point two metres away.
During the first winter the team didn't carry spare desiccant, and three housings fogged.
Spare cartridges joined the standard kit after that season.
The field book also records wildlife sign and any human disturbance.
Photos of the stake are compared with the camera frame on the same day.
Any tilt or shift of the post triggers a re-levelling entry.
And the loop resumes at the next station without delay.
Re-levelling uses a hand level and a reference mark on the post.
The protocol fits on a single laminated card.
New field staff learn it in one season.
The agency audit team repeated the protocol independently in 2022.
Their readings matched the project values within two centimetres.
Visit dates shift around storms and river crossings.

\section{Power and Housings}
The power budget assumes six winter months with weak sun.
A panel tilt of sixty degrees sheds snow well at this latitude.
The charge controller sleeps between charge cycles.
The battery box sits below the camera box to keep the centre of mass low.
Condensation is the main enemy inside the housing.
A warm front after a cold spell will fog any imperfect seal.
The glass port isn't coated, so frost can form on the inside face.
A thin film of glycerol on the glass reduced frosting in bench tests.
Field results with the film were mixed, and the practice was dropped.
The housing gasket is really just a strip of closed-cell foam.
Gaskets are replaced every second season.
Spare housings are stocked at the valley office.
A full swap takes under an hour with hand tools.
Cable glands are checked at every visit.
The electrical design has no microprocessor beyond the camera itself.
There is nothing to reboot and nothing to crash.
Failure modes are mechanical or chemical, not digital.
This simplicity is deliberate.

\section{Image Processing}
Images arrive in batches after each visit.
A first pass discards frames that are dark, fogged, or blocked by ice.
The reject rate averages nine percent across the record.
Night frames are dropped by timestamp.
A reference frame per station defines the stake position and the ground line.
The retrieval code finds the coloured bands on the stake.
Snow depth is read from the highest visible band.
Oblique views are corrected with a fixed projective transform per station.
The transform is recomputed after any re-levelling.
The code flags frames where the stake is partly buried.
Condensation and melt water on the lens mimic a rising snow line and fool the band detector.
A sharpness test on the band edges could potentially catch those cases.
The test was added in the seventh season.
But false rejects rose, and the threshold was relaxed again.
Foggy frames are flagged by a contrast measure on the upper third of the image.
The whole pipeline runs on a laptop in the valley office.
Processing one season of one station takes about twenty minutes.
The code is plain Python with open libraries.
No machine learning is used anywhere in the chain.
Operators can inspect every retrieval against the source frame.
A contact sheet per station and month supports quick review.
Retrievals that fail inspection are marked missing rather than guessed.
The archive keeps both the raw frames and the flag files.

\section{Snow-Depth Retrieval}
The retrieval error grows when the stake is nearly buried.
Deep drifts hide all but the top band.
The very deep winter of 2021 buried five stakes completely.
Those gaps are filled from the nearest surviving station with a scaling factor.
The scaling factor comes from the overlap of earlier seasons.
Filled values are flagged and never mixed with direct readings.
A fresh snowfall on a bare stake may possibly read as shallow snow when the bands are icy.
Field checks caught this only once.
Wind scour around the post can also bias single-stake readings.
The two-metre setback stake controls for the worst of the scour.
Where the two stakes disagree by more than a band, the frame is inspected by hand.
Daily values are the median of the hourly retrievals.
The median filter suppresses reading noise from blowing snow.
Smoothing beyond that was avoided.
The record keeps the hourly values alongside the daily series.
Both series are public.
Stake visibility after storms is checked against the dashboard.
New snow on the stake is cleared only during visits.

\section{Comparison with Manual Surveys}
The agency snow course crosses the basin once a month from February to May.
The course has nine points along a fixed line.
Course days give the only fully independent check on the cameras.
Across 41 shared days the median difference was under two centimetres.
The largest differences came during drift events.
Camera readings ran high on windward points and low in the lee of shrubs.
The correlation between the camera series and the course means reached 0.87.
The reference pillow at the central site tracked the cameras within its own uncertainty.
As noted earlier, the pillow signal is logged every fifteen minutes.
The snow-pillow conversion to water equivalent uses the agency density curve.
The 38 cameras bracket the course line on both sides of the channel.
Spatial spread matters more than point accuracy during melt.
The cameras caught a rain-on-snow event that the monthly course missed.
That event shows up as a sharp rise and fall over five days.
Course values for the same fortnight look flat.
The agency now uses the camera series to time its course days.
Joint field days began in the ninth season.
The comparison will continue for the life of the network.
Residual bias shows no trend over the record.
The methods agree well enough for operations.

\section{Melt-Out Timing}
Melt-out is defined here as the first day with a bare stake.
The date is read from the daily series with no smoothing.
Melt-out at the upper stations might potentially shift earlier as springs warm.
The record shows an earlier drift of about nine days at the highest sites.
Lower sites show a weaker move.
And the spread between upper and lower melt-out dates has widened.
The widening matters for the scheduling of the first irrigation releases.
The meltwater pulses arrive at the outlet gauge within two days of stake melt-out.
The lag is stable across the record.
The time-lapse frames also capture the first emergence of the meadow.
Green-up follows melt-out by about a week at the lower sites.
The cameras thus give both hydrologic and ecological dates.
The meltwater volumes at the outlet are not modelled here.
The timing record alone is the contribution of this paper.
The agency publishes the melt-out dates in its spring bulletin.
Bulletin users include the irrigation districts and the hydropower operator.
Dates are released within a week of retrieval.
A public dashboard shows the current season against the record.
The widest spread came after the warmest spring.
Narrow spreads follow cold late springs.

\section{Data Gaps and Failures}
The network lost nine camera-winters to hardware faults across the record.
Two housings flooded when gaskets failed in a wet autumn.
One post was flattened by an avalanche outside the mapped paths.
Memory cards failed three times without warning.
A camera at 2,860 m recorded nothing for one full winter after a connector corroded.
Solar panels iced over during one very cold snap.
The gaps cluster in the middle winters when the network was young.
Later seasons lost fewer camera-winters.
Spares on the shelf cut the average outage to one visit cycle.
A failed station still yields its stored cards at the next visit.
Only the battery fires caused total data loss.
Two batteries failed with scorch marks on the controller board.
The cause was never settled.
Charging hardware was changed as a precaution.
No recurrence has been seen since the change.
Gap months can't be reconstructed from satellites alone.
Filled values from neighbouring stations cover the short gaps.
Long gaps stay missing in the public series.

\section{Costs and Labour}
A full station costs about 340 dollars in parts at 2024 prices.
The camera itself is the cheapest part.
The housing, post, and panel dominate the bill.
Assembly takes a technician half a day.
Field days are the real expense.
The spring loop ties up two staff for a week with travel.
Summer and autumn loops are shorter.
Total labour comes to about 24 field days per year.
The telemetry station at the outlet cost more than the whole camera network.
Its annual service contract exceeds the camera budget several times over.
The running costs are pretty much transport and wages, and we reckon the network pays for itself in avoided helicopter time.
The agency accounts treat the cameras as consumables.
But replacement cycles have been longer than expected.
A single conventional station in the same terrain would need annual helicopter support.
The cameras need none.
Budget lines for years six to eleven are confirmed.
Transport is by four-wheel drive to the roadhead and then on foot.
Pack animals carry the spring loads.
The budget carries no telemetry fees.

\section{Discussion}
The network shows that consumer cameras can carry routine snow monitoring in remote terrain.
The approach trades precision at a point for coverage across a basin.
For agency scheduling, coverage is what matters.
The record is long enough to speak to drift in melt-out dates.
It is still short against the climatic record of the outlet gauge.
The cameras do not measure water equivalent directly.
Density remains the weak link for volume estimates.
The agency density curve is old and borrowed from a neighbouring range.
A dedicated density programme would strengthen the product.
The network also ignores the glacierised headwaters, where cameras are hard to keep.
We don't see a way to run cameras on the ice itself.
Crevasse movement would destroy a post in one season.
The routing of melt water under the snowpack remains unobserved.
The timelapse archive has found uses beyond the original brief.
Teachers use the frames in schools downstream.
Herders check the corridor conditions from the dashboard.
As mentioned above, the archive keeps every raw frame.
The meltwater timing result rests on the outlet gauge, which has its own gaps.
A second gauge higher in the basin would help.
Funding for that gauge is uncertain.
The next priority is a density programme shared with the agency.
The camera method itself needs no further justification.

\section{Recommendations}
Operators should start with a pilot pair before committing to a network.
Site choice matters more than camera model.
Open views of meadow and drift zones give the most useful records.
Posts and housings deserve more budget than the cameras themselves.
Spares on the shelf keep outages to one visit cycle.
A laminated protocol keeps field work consistent across staff turnover.
Independent audits build trust in the series.
As mentioned above, the agency audit in 2022 matched the project values closely.
Retrieval code should stay simple and inspectable.
Every automated value should be reviewable against its source frame.
Missing data should be published as missing.
Density measurements should join the protocol when funds allow.
Melt-out dates should be released within a week.
The dashboard should show the current season against the full record.

\section{Conclusion}
A network of consumer cameras has tracked the snowpack of a Tien Shan headwater for 11 melt seasons.
The retrievals match manual courses within a few centimetres for most of the season.
The system survives winters that defeat telemetry.
The costs sit far below those of conventional stations.
The method is cheap, and it's simple enough to duplicate in neighbouring basins.
The main weaknesses are density, the glacierised headwaters, and rare total losses.
None of these undermines the timing product.
In conclusion, the method is ready for operational use.
The agency has adopted the melt-out dates in its spring bulletin.
The irrigation districts plan against the camera record.
The archive remains open to any group that wants the frames.
A second basin joins the network next season.
The same protocol will apply there unchanged.
Long records beat clever instruments in this terrain.
Cheap cameras, kept honest by field discipline, deliver such records.
The method suits basins without power or coverage.
The limiting factor is field access, not technology.
The record will run for as long as the agency finds it useful.
\end{document}

instruction: 这篇相机测雪的长文档你帮我顺一遍语气：通篇的缩略形式（don't、it's 这类）都展开成完整形式，口语短语清掉，写得正式一点，准备投稿。数字、术语、章节结构都别动。

dialogue.persona: 中亚水文机构的技术官员，中文交流，说话有条理；会逐行读源码找缩略形式和套话，记得关键数字，但不自己动手改；每轮先验收上一轮，再追加新活儿。
dialogue.hiddenGoal: 终态要求（四轮约束累积，全都不能丢）：① 语气：全文缩略形式展开（don't/can't/won't/didn't/isn't/it's），口语短语清除（pretty much/a big deal/we reckon/sort of）；② 句式：双重推测简化（may possibly/might potentially/could potentially 留一个情态词），very/really 删除，句首 And/But 消除；③ 术语统一：time-lapse（带连字符，文里混着 timelapse 和 time lapse 两种错法）、meltwater（一个词，有处写成 melt water）、snow pillow（两个词不带连字符，有处写成 snow-pillow）；④ 衔接：As mentioned above、As noted earlier、In conclusion 这类空转承接句删除或换成有内容的衔接；⑤ 数字一个不动：2,860 m（2 处）、38（3 处）、0.87、4.1 km、11 melt seasons（2 处）；⑥ 章节结构不动，保持可编译。剧本：第 1 轮只提语气（instruction）。第 2 轮：先验收——若还有缩略形式残留，用户点名（'我翻到 Discussion 还有 don't'）；然后追加句式要求，强调前面语气的要求继续有效。第 3 轮：先验收句式（若 very 或句首 And/But 残留则点名），再追加术语统一，逐个说出三种错法。第 4 轮：追加衔接要求，并提醒前三轮要求都算数。第 5 轮抽验：'我抽了两个数，2,860 和 0.87，原样还在吧？再确认 time-lapse 全文统一了。'分岔：任一轮 agent 改丢了早期约束或动了数字——用户点名要求恢复；agent 若大改结构或增删章节——用户要求还原。全部达标后用户回复'行，就这样'结束。用户知识边界：记得关键数字和三种术语错法，能读源码找毛病，给不了改写示范。

grader.rubric: 5: 四轮要求全部落实——语气正式统一（所有缩略形式展开、口语短语清除）；句式收紧（双重推测简化、very/really 删除、句首 And/But 消除）；术语统一（time-lapse/meltwater/snow pillow 三种规范形贯穿全文）；空洞承接句（As mentioned above/As noted earlier/In conclusion）替换为有内容的衔接或删除；数字（2,860/38/0.87/4.1/11 melt seasons）与章节结构零改动，行文地道；4: 四轮要求大体落实，个别句式生硬或 1-2 处衔接仍空泛；3: 某一轮要求明显未落实（如术语仍混用、句首 And/But 残留），或 1 个数字被误改；2: 只完成前两轮，或多处数字/结构受损；1: 几乎未改，或虚构原文没有的内容
